title: MTA-STS (RFC 8461): the other half of SMTP transport security
description:
## The question

Does the workspace need MTA-STS now that RFC 7672 SMTP DANE is done?

## Evidence: the two camps barely overlap

Probed 2026-11-24 via 9.9.9.9.

MTA-STS published (_mta-sts TXT):
  fastmail.com   v=STSv1; id=20260728T132000
  gmail.com      v=STSv1; id=20190429T010101
  outlook.com    v=STSv1; id=20190225000000Z
  debian.org     (none)

DANE published (TLSA on the MX host):
  debian.org, freebsd.org, huque.com, nlnetlabs.nl -- all yes
  fastmail.com -- no, and CANNOT: neither fastmail.com nor messagingengine.com has a DS record, so the MX zone is unsigned and DANE is impossible there rather than merely unpublished

That last point is the one worth internalising: DANE depends on the MX HOST zone being signed, not the envelope domain. RFC 7672 section 2.2.1 treats the MX RRset security and the TLSA base domain security as separate questions, and Fastmail is a clean example of why.

So a sending MTA that implements only DANE cannot protect mail to Gmail, Outlook or Fastmail -- which is most mail by volume. The large consumer providers chose MTA-STS; the DNSSEC-committed infrastructure domains chose DANE.

## RFC 8461 gives us a MUST NOT that lands on code already written

Section 2, verbatim:

  "senders who implement MTA-STS validation MUST NOT allow MTA-STS Policy
   validation to override a failing DANE validation."

SmtpDaneVerdict is already the right shape for this: an MTA must consult DANE first and must not let an MTA-STS success rescue a Failed. rfc7672_permits_delivery() is the hook. Worth asserting in a test once MTA-STS exists, because it is the one place the two mechanisms can be combined wrongly.

## Proposed shape, mirroring the DANE split

pkix-mta-sts (no_std core, pure):
- policy file parsing -- a simple key/value text format per section 3.2
- the "mx" pattern match, including the single leading *. wildcard rule
- mode handling: none / testing / enforce
- policy ID comparison for refresh decisions
- max_age handling as data, no clock of its own (take now_unix, as the rest of the workspace does)

A std adapter for discovery:
- the _mta-sts.<domain> TXT lookup
- the HTTPS GET of https://mta-sts.<domain>/.well-known/mta-sts.txt
- certificate validation of that fetch, which is genuinely PKIX work and should go through pkix-chain::verify_tls_server rather than a bespoke path
- the SSRF considerations from pkix-aia-http apply directly: the URL is derived from a remote-supplied domain. The literal-host pre-check added there for reqwest is the kind of hole to avoid repeating.
- policy caching. Policies carry max_age up to a year and caching is load-bearing for the threat model, so this needs a caller-supplied cache: the workspace does not touch the filesystem (PKIX-j32w.5).

## The honest caveat, which the docs must carry

MTA-STS is a WEAKER threat model than DANE and should not be presented as equivalent. Its trust roots are the Web PKI plus an UNSIGNED DNS TXT record, so first contact is trust-on-first-use and the protection comes from caching. RFC 8461 section 1 says so directly -- it "does not require DNSSEC, at a cost of risking malicious downgrades" -- and section 10.2 notes that resistance to this class of downgrade "is a feature of DANE, due to its use of DNSSEC for policy discovery."

That is a reason to implement it, not a reason to refuse: it is deployable where DNSSEC is not, which is most of the mail system. But a consumer should be able to tell from the API which of the two authenticated a connection, the same way SmtpDaneVerdict distinguishes NotApplicable from Authenticated.

## Non-negotiable #5 check

RFC 8461 is IETF standards track, so this is a standards-body spec the workspace commits to rather than a vendor policy. No tension there.

## Acceptance

[ ] Decide whether to build it at all, and record the decision either way
[ ] If yes: pkix-mta-sts no_std core with policy parsing, mx matching and mode handling
[ ] If yes: a std adapter for TXT lookup and the HTTPS policy fetch, reusing pkix-chain for certificate validation and honouring the pkix-aia-http SSRF lessons
[ ] If yes: a test asserting MTA-STS cannot override a failing DANE validation (RFC 8461 section 2)
[ ] If yes: documentation stating plainly that the trust model is weaker than DANE and why
close_reason:
DECIDED AND BUILT 2026-11-25. Answer to "do we need MTA-STS in the PKIX workspace": yes, the policy core and the DANE precedence rule. Not the discovery adapter, which is deliberately deferred.

## The decision

MTA-STS is weaker than DANE and that is not a reason to refuse it. RFC 8461 §1 trades DNSSEC for the Web PKI "at a cost of risking malicious downgrades", and §10.2 names the lost property. A policy is authenticated by CAs plus an UNSIGNED TXT record, so first contact is trust-on-first-use and the protection comes from caching for up to a year.

It ships because it deploys where DNSSEC does not, which is most of the mail system. Gmail, Outlook and Fastmail publish MTA-STS policies; a DANE-only sender protects none of that mail. The workspace already had SMTP DANE end to end, so the gap was the half of SMTP transport security that actually covers the large providers.

What the documentation does NOT do is imply parity. Both the crate docs and the README state the trust model plainly, and SmtpTransportSecurity keeps the mechanisms as separate variants rather than collapsing to a boolean, so a consumer can tag or route on which one authenticated a connection.

## What shipped

pkix-mta-sts (no_std, 0.1.0, 36 tests). §3.2 policy parsing, §4.1 MX matching, §5 policy application. No DNS, no HTTP, no clock -- the caller passes the fetched text in, as pkix-dane takes TLSA records. PolicyOutcome separates the delivery decision from the validation fact, because testing mode exists precisely to make them differ.

pkix-identity::dns_name_matches_pattern. §4.1 defines MX matching as RFC 6125's rule restricted so '*' matches only the entire left-most label, which is matches_dns_san exactly. Exposed rather than restated: a second copy of security-relevant wildcard matching is a divergence hazard, and a test asserts the two agree.

pkix-chain::combine_smtp_transport_security (feature mta-sts, implies dane, 8 tests). §2's "MUST NOT allow MTA-STS Policy validation to override a failing DANE validation", as code rather than a convention.

## Three things worth keeping

READ THE ABNF, DO NOT INFER IT. sts-policy-max-age-value = 1*10(DIGIT). The first implementation used u64::from_str, which accepts a leading '+' and underscores -- non-conforming. Only reading the grammar caught it. The same read showed every keyword carries RFC 7405's %s prefix, meaning case-SENSITIVE, which the implementation deliberately deviates from (below).

WHICH DIRECTION DOES STRICTNESS FAIL? Keywords are matched case-insensitively although the ABNF is case-sensitive. A policy whose only defect is "mode: Enforce" is unambiguous about what the domain wants; rejecting it reports NO POLICY, and a sender with no policy applies no protection. Leniency yields enforce, strictness yields plaintext. The deviation is documented, tested, and the test says why so it cannot be "fixed" into strictness without someone reading the reason. max_age is NOT lenient, because there strictness costs nothing.

NON-EXHAUSTIVE ENUMS ARE A SAFETY PROMPT. combine_smtp_transport_security reads PolicyOutcome::mta_sts_permits_delivery rather than matching variants, so a variant added later that forbids delivery still forbids it. A variant-by-variant match compiled fine and would have silently permitted it; the non_exhaustive compile error is what surfaced the question.

Also: two SMTP mechanisms, two different correct profiles. §4.2 requires a SAN, so BasicTlsProfile is right for MTA-STS -- the opposite of SMTP DANE, where RFC 7672 §3.2.3 consults commonName and BasicSmtpMtaProfile requires neither SAN nor EKU. Choosing the wrong one fails real mail. Recorded in both crates' docs.

## Acceptance

[x] Decide whether to build it at all, and record the decision either way
[x] pkix-mta-sts no_std core with policy parsing, mx matching and mode handling
[ ] A std adapter for TXT lookup and the HTTPS policy fetch -- DEFERRED, filed separately
[x] A test asserting MTA-STS cannot override a failing DANE validation
[x] Documentation stating plainly that the trust model is weaker than DANE

## Why the adapter is deferred rather than skipped

It is a different kind of work: a resolver, an HTTPS client, a policy cache with §5.1's control flow, SSRF considerations on a caller-influenced hostname, and §3.3's text/plain media-type check. None of it is hard, but none of it is the policy logic, and bundling them would have made a large change where two reviewable ones fit. The core is useful without it to anyone who already has an HTTP client.
